technique: the turn — the exact line where picture becomes meaning, and how the poem earns it
lesson:
Today we work on one technique: the turn. The turn is the line where a poem stops describing a scene and tells you what the scene was about. It gives you the picture first, then the meaning.

Here the poem spends most of its length on plain work. "The handle of the spade has gone the color of your palm." "earth packed down with the flat of the blade." These are things you can see and touch. Then it turns: "There are bulbs you tucked into the dark that are counting on the light you're about to let in." That line says what the digging meant. It was about hope and waiting.

It works because you watch the work first, so the meaning lands on something solid. You trust it.

Try this: write your scene plainly, then add one line that says what it was for.

The second time through, listen for how the last words, "So — up!", answer that turn.

Here is the poem.
poem:
The handle of the spade has gone the color of your palm by now,
worn smooth where the grain gave way to use, a thing
your hand finds in the dark without being told.
You carry it out past the fence, breath hanging,
the ground gone hard enough overnight to argue back—
a good stubbornness, the kind you don't mind meeting.
There's a satisfaction in a hole dug to the right depth,
deep as the thing you're burying asks to go,
earth packed down with the flat of the blade and left.
You've put a season's worth of small faith underground
this week, three fingers deep and then some,
and nothing about it shows yet, nor should.
Inside, the kettle's got a word or two to say.

There are bulbs you tucked into the dark that are counting on the light you're about to let in—

So — up!
